display_name: Penfolds Bin 2 Mataro, South Eastern Australia
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Bin 2 is Penfolds’ long-running Shiraz-Mataro blend, built to turn warm South Australian fruit into a red that is more savory and structured than straight-ahead jammy Shiraz. In the glass, that means McLaren Vale’s dark, plush fruit gets tightened by Mourvèdre’s game, earth, and firmer tannin, giving you a bottle that drinks like barbecue-season Australia with more grip than people expect.",
  "wine_summary": "This wine matters because it sits in a useful lane that many large brands ignore: broadly available, regionally anchored South Australian red with a clear varietal idea rather than a generic rich blend. Bin 2 has been associated with the Shiraz-Mataro partnership for decades, and that pairing makes sense in McLaren Vale. Shiraz brings blackberry, plum, pepper, and body; Mataro contributes leathery, ferrous, sometimes olive-toned savor and a more sinewy frame. The result is not subtle for subtlety’s sake. It is built around flavor contrast.\n\nMcLaren Vale gives this style a strong base. The region stretches from Gulf St Vincent to the Mount Lofty foothills, so vines can feel both maritime influence from the west and warmer inland conditions as sites move eastward and upward. Key soils include red-brown earth, terra rossa over limestone, rendzina, sand, and dark cracking clay, and each pushes the blend in a slightly different direction: limestone-based soils tend to preserve line and lift, while clay holds water and supports darker, fuller fruit in warm years. For a wine sold under the wider South Eastern Australia designation but tied here to McLaren Vale, the important takeaway is stylistic: ripe black fruit, supple texture, and enough savory detail from Mataro to keep the wine from turning flat or confectionary.",
  "terroir_expression": "McLaren Vale’s geology is useful precisely because it is mixed. Terra rossa over limestone and rendzina soils often give red wines better shape because limestone can help moderate vine vigor and keep acidity from collapsing in a warm region; that is part of why the fruit can taste rich without losing all definition. Red-brown earth and dark cracking clay push the wine toward blacker fruit, broader mid-palate weight, and the chocolate-licorice side of warm-climate Shiraz. Add the Gulf St Vincent cooling effect and you get nights that can slow sugar accumulation just enough to keep pepper, olive, and meat notes in play. In Bin 2, place reads as ripe blackberry and plum first, then a savory undercurrent of dried herbs, leather, and game that points to both Mataro and the region’s warm, dry Mediterranean pattern.",
  "vinification_summary": "Penfolds is known for a house style that favors consistency, full flavor, and polish, so Bin 2 is typically made to be reliable rather than site-transparent in the single-vineyard sense. The likely approach is straightforward warm-climate red winemaking: fully ripe fruit, fermentation for color and tannin extraction, then maturation in oak to round edges and add spice. Oak matters here because it does more than add flavor; it also allows slow oxygen exchange, which softens tannins over time and helps knit Shiraz’s plush fruit to Mataro’s drier structure. The blend itself is the key cellar decision. Shiraz alone could drift toward sweetness of impression at 14.5% alcohol, while Mataro brings the savory snap and tannic drag that keep the finish drier.",
  "food_pairing": "Texas-style smoked brisket with black pepper bark — the wine’s ripe fruit can handle the smoke, while Shiraz’s pepper note and Mataro’s meaty savor lock onto the bark and rendered fat.\nNashville hot chicken — high alcohol and dense fruit cushion the heat, and the tannin gives the fried crust something to grip.\nLamb kofta with sumac yogurt and charred eggplant — this is where the wine’s olive, leather, and spice notes make sense; the savory profile meets the lamb head-on, and the yogurt cools the finish.\nDuck breast with blackberry jus and roasted beetroot — the fruit in the sauce mirrors the wine’s blackberry-plum core, while the earthy beetroot fits the Mataro side.\nBraised beef cheek with celeriac purée and roasted shallots — slow-cooked collagen softens under the wine’s tannin, and the dish has enough depth to match the wine’s weight without drowning its savory detail.",
  "comparable_wines": "d'Arenberg The Stump Jump GSM — comparable because it delivers warm South Australian dark fruit with a savory Rhône-variety edge at a similar broad-market level.\nTorbreck Woodcutter's Shiraz — comparable for plush South Australian Shiraz fruit, though Bin 2 is usually more gamey and structured because of the Mataro.\nYangarra Shiraz — comparable as a McLaren Vale benchmark, but more site-driven and fresher in profile; Bin 2 is broader, oakier, and more about house style consistency.",
  "style_profile": "Full-bodied dry red with moderate tannin and savory Shiraz-Mataro depth",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink now through the near term, especially for 2007-2013 vintages that have already had time to integrate. Store at a stable cool temperature and open 30 minutes early; this style benefits more from air than from long further aging.",
  "value_assessment": "$20-35 is the zone where Bin 2 usually makes sense. Against d'Arenberg The Stump Jump GSM and Peter Lehmann The Barossan Shiraz, it offers more savory complexity than many supermarket-level Australian reds, though it is not the sharpest value if you want freshness over heft. It is worth buying if you want a dependable, fuller-bodied red with some earth and game in the mix rather than pure sweet-fruit impact.",
  "market_position": "This is built for retail shelves, steakhouse by-the-bottle lists, and drinkers who know the Penfolds name but do not want to pay Bin-series flagship money. It fits the customer who wants a serious weeknight red or barbecue red, not the collector chasing rarity. In restaurants, it works best where the list needs a recognizable Australian label with enough structure for lamb, beef, and smoke-driven dishes.",
  "insider_take": "Think of it as the anti-fruit-bomb Australian red. People see Shiraz from warm South Australia and expect simple sweetness; the Mataro changes that, adding a savory, slightly rugged edge that is the whole point of the bottle. Skip it if you want freshness and lift in the Northern Rhône mold, but buy it if you want dark fruit with barbecue-friendly grip and no need to overthink the occasion.",

parsed.hook: Bin 2 is Penfolds’ long-running Shiraz-Mataro blend, built to turn warm South Australian fruit into a red that is more savory and structured than straight-ahead jammy Shiraz. In the glass, that means McLaren Vale’s dark, plush fruit gets tightened by Mourvèdre’s game, earth, and firmer tannin, giving you a bottle that drinks like barbecue-season Australia with more grip than people expect.
parsed.wine_summary:
This wine matters because it sits in a useful lane that many large brands ignore: broadly available, regionally anchored South Australian red with a clear varietal idea rather than a generic rich blend. Bin 2 has been associated with the Shiraz-Mataro partnership for decades, and that pairing makes sense in McLaren Vale. Shiraz brings blackberry, plum, pepper, and body; Mataro contributes leathery, ferrous, sometimes olive-toned savor and a more sinewy frame. The result is not subtle for subtlety’s sake. It is built around flavor contrast.

McLaren Vale gives this style a strong base. The region stretches from Gulf St Vincent to the Mount Lofty foothills, so vines can feel both maritime influence from the west and warmer inland conditions as sites move eastward and upward. Key soils include red-brown earth, terra rossa over limestone, rendzina, sand, and dark cracking clay, and each pushes the blend in a slightly different direction: limestone-based soils tend to preserve line and lift, while clay holds water and supports darker, fuller fruit in warm years. For a wine sold under the wider South Eastern Australia designation but tied here to McLaren Vale, the important takeaway is stylistic: ripe black fruit, supple texture, and enough savory detail from Mataro to keep the wine from turning flat or confectionary.
parsed.terroir_expression: McLaren Vale’s geology is useful precisely because it is mixed. Terra rossa over limestone and rendzina soils often give red wines better shape because limestone can help moderate vine vigor and keep acidity from collapsing in a warm region; that is part of why the fruit can taste rich without losing all definition. Red-brown earth and dark cracking clay push the wine toward blacker fruit, broader mid-palate weight, and the chocolate-licorice side of warm-climate Shiraz. Add the Gulf St Vincent cooling effect and you get nights that can slow sugar accumulation just enough to keep pepper, olive, and meat notes in play. In Bin 2, place reads as ripe blackberry and plum first, then a savory undercurrent of dried herbs, leather, and game that points to both Mataro and the region’s warm, dry Mediterranean pattern.
parsed.vinification_summary: Penfolds is known for a house style that favors consistency, full flavor, and polish, so Bin 2 is typically made to be reliable rather than site-transparent in the single-vineyard sense. The likely approach is straightforward warm-climate red winemaking: fully ripe fruit, fermentation for color and tannin extraction, then maturation in oak to round edges and add spice. Oak matters here because it does more than add flavor; it also allows slow oxygen exchange, which softens tannins over time and helps knit Shiraz’s plush fruit to Mataro’s drier structure. The blend itself is the key cellar decision. Shiraz alone could drift toward sweetness of impression at 14.5% alcohol, while Mataro brings the savory snap and tannic drag that keep the finish drier.
parsed.food_pairing:
Texas-style smoked brisket with black pepper bark — the wine’s ripe fruit can handle the smoke, while Shiraz’s pepper note and Mataro’s meaty savor lock onto the bark and rendered fat.
Nashville hot chicken — high alcohol and dense fruit cushion the heat, and the tannin gives the fried crust something to grip.
Lamb kofta with sumac yogurt and charred eggplant — this is where the wine’s olive, leather, and spice notes make sense; the savory profile meets the lamb head-on, and the yogurt cools the finish.
Duck breast with blackberry jus and roasted beetroot — the fruit in the sauce mirrors the wine’s blackberry-plum core, while the earthy beetroot fits the Mataro side.
Braised beef cheek with celeriac purée and roasted shallots — slow-cooked collagen softens under the wine’s tannin, and the dish has enough depth to match the wine’s weight without drowning its savory detail.
parsed.comparable_wines:
d'Arenberg The Stump Jump GSM — comparable because it delivers warm South Australian dark fruit with a savory Rhône-variety edge at a similar broad-market level.
Torbreck Woodcutter's Shiraz — comparable for plush South Australian Shiraz fruit, though Bin 2 is usually more gamey and structured because of the Mataro.
Yangarra Shiraz — comparable as a McLaren Vale benchmark, but more site-driven and fresher in profile; Bin 2 is broader, oakier, and more about house style consistency.
parsed.style_profile: Full-bodied dry red with moderate tannin and savory Shiraz-Mataro depth
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink now through the near term, especially for 2007-2013 vintages that have already had time to integrate. Store at a stable cool temperature and open 30 minutes early; this style benefits more from air than from long further aging.
parsed.value_assessment: $20-35 is the zone where Bin 2 usually makes sense. Against d'Arenberg The Stump Jump GSM and Peter Lehmann The Barossan Shiraz, it offers more savory complexity than many supermarket-level Australian reds, though it is not the sharpest value if you want freshness over heft. It is worth buying if you want a dependable, fuller-bodied red with some earth and game in the mix rather than pure sweet-fruit impact.
parsed.market_position: This is built for retail shelves, steakhouse by-the-bottle lists, and drinkers who know the Penfolds name but do not want to pay Bin-series flagship money. It fits the customer who wants a serious weeknight red or barbecue red, not the collector chasing rarity. In restaurants, it works best where the list needs a recognizable Australian label with enough structure for lamb, beef, and smoke-driven dishes.
parsed.insider_take: Think of it as the anti-fruit-bomb Australian red. People see Shiraz from warm South Australia and expect simple sweetness; the Mataro changes that, adding a savory, slightly rugged edge that is the whole point of the bottle. Skip it if you want freshness and lift in the Northern Rhône mold, but buy it if you want dark fruit with barbecue-friendly grip and no need to overthink the occasion.
